docs.title: Streamhouse Customer 360
docs.text:
Synchronize a change in business state everywhere it is used: from a database transaction, through Kafka and Flink on Confluent Cloud, to the data lake and to the applications and AI agents that depend on it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The purpose of this repository is to implement a Customer 360 streaming data pipeline that integrates operational databases (PostgreSQL, DB2, etc.) with event streaming, Change Data Capture (CDC), and modern lakehouse analytical sinks.

This is one possible demonstration of the Streamhouse architecture with Confluent Cloud products.

The home page of the application to drive the demonstration

From a business requirement point of view, the goal is to demonstrate how to synchronize a change in business state everywhere it is used.

The user story for the demonstration is:

As a data architect, I want to deliver business entity updates to every system and person that depends on them, at the same time, so that no team operates on a stale or conflicting copy of that fact.

The Streamhouse data architecture continuously captures and processes changes as they happen, governs that data, and makes the same trusted business context available to applications, agents, and analytics without requiring additional data copies and pipelines.

At a high level, the Streamhouse reference architecture looks like the figure below:

Streamhouse Capabilities

The architecture provides a capture layer that brings data into a centralized messaging platform, which transports and persists records defined by structured schemas. A layer of transformation, data enrichment, and data analytics constructs serves golden records to downstream processing. Those golden records, which represent valuable business events or data analytics products, can be consumed by AI agents to build their own fresh context.

When the architecture is applied to the Confluent technology stack, Streamhouse is supported by the following components:

Streamhouse With Confluent Cloud
  1. Capture is done by different Kafka source connectors.
  2. Transport is supported by Kafka brokers and topics, with contracts in Schema Registry.
  3. Transform is done by Confluent Cloud for Flink, with stateless or stateful logic to build golden records and business events.
  4. Serve is supported by Flink snapshot queries, Kafka sink connectors, and Tableflow, which writes Iceberg tables to object storage. The Real-Time Context Engine is also a serving layer for AI agents and interactive Jupyter data science notebooks.
  5. Governance is done by Schema Registry and other end-to-end governance capabilities.

docs.title: Shifting to real-time processing
docs.text:
Preparing medallion layers is possible by using data already in Kafka. The classical batch processing can be shifted to the left of the architecture by doing transformation, filtering, and deduplication to build the silver layer in Kafka topics using Flink processing.

The business logic that applies to data in Kafka topics and Flink tables can be built in Flink to create gold records. Those gold records, representing dimensions and facts, can be persisted long term in object storage as Iceberg tables. External query engines and a federated catalog can be used on top of those Iceberg tables. Most of the logic done in batch should be easily ported to real-time processing. Still, some considerations like state size, always-on streaming processing, time, and watermarks add to the semantic complexity.

Adopting an event-driven architecture, silver and gold topics/ business events are reusable and not just usable for analytic query engines.

docs.title: CDC envelope automatic processing to upsert tables
docs.text:
When tables are created by the Debezium connector, their changelog.mode is set to retract if the source table in the SQL database has no primary key.

WITH (
  'changelog.mode' = 'retract',
  'kafka.cleanup-policy' = 'delete',
  'key.format' = 'avro-registry',
  'scan.startup.mode' = 'earliest-offset',
  'value.format' = 'avro-debezium-registry'
)

It is still possible to alter the default settings so developers can work on the CDC envelope and operation. This pattern is demonstrated for cdc.public.customers in this SQL:

 SELECT
    customer_id,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.first_name, after.first_name), 'NULL') as first_name,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.last_name, after.last_name), 'NULL') as last_name,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.email, after.email), 'NULL') as email,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.phone, after.phone), 'NULL') as phone,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.date_of_birth, after.date_of_birth), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as date_of_birth,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.gender, after.gender), 'NULL') as gender,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.created_at, after.created_at), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as registration_date,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.segment, after.segment), 'NULL')   as customer_segment,
    TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(IF(op= 'd', before.customer_since, after.customer_since), 'yyyy-MM-dd''T''HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS''Z''') as customer_since,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.city, after.city), 'NULL') as city,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.state, after.state), 'NULL') as state,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.postal_code, after.postal_code), 'NULL') as postal_code,
    coalesce(IF(op= 'd', before.country, after.country), 'NULL') as country,
    `$rowtime` as event_ts
    FROM {{ source('cdc', 'customers') }}

docs.title: Lateral snapshot join on slow-moving, seeded data
docs.text:
A common data enrichment pattern is to join streaming records with reference data, which changes less frequently. There are multiple ways to support this integration, but in Confluent Cloud it is best to deploy the reference data in a Kafka topic so it can be reused for any enrichment. The new lateral snapshot feature in Flink helps with these kinds of joins.

The reference data is defined in the pipelines/seeds folder as a set of two csv files, and deployed simply by running: 

dbt seed

The resulting Kafka topics, and schemas are created in Confluent Cloud.

  • seeds/country_codes.csv has 249 ISO 3166-1 countries with alpha-2 code, alpha-3 code, numeric code, and name. The country_code key matches customers.country.
  • seeds/currency_codes.csv has 178 ISO 4217 currencies with code, numeric code, and name. The currency_code key matches transactions.currency.
  • seeds/seeds.yml adds descriptions, plus unique and not_null tests on the two key columns.

The snapshot lateral join query is implemented in the transaction CDC processing with the following example:

WITH card_account AS (
  select 
    a.account_id, 
    a.customer_id, 
    a.balance as account_balance, 
    a.credit_limit as account_credit_limit,
    c.card_id,
    c.card_brand, 
    c.card_type, 
    c.has_chip, 
    c.credit_limit as card_credit_limit
    from {{ ref('src_accounts') }}  as a 
    JOIN LATERAL SNAPSHOT(
        input => TABLE  {{ ref('src_cards') }},
        n_time => DESCRIPTOR($rowtime),
        load_completed_idle_timeout => INTERVAL '1' MINUTE
    ) AS c
    ON a.account_id = c.account_id
    )

Another example to get join from seed reference data:

    SELECT
        t.*,
        cur.currency_code_numeric,
        cur.currency_name
    FROM relevant_tx AS t
    LEFT JOIN LATERAL SNAPSHOT(
        input => TABLE {{ ref('currency_codes') }},
        on_time => DESCRIPTOR($rowtime),
        load_completed_idle_timeout => INTERVAL '30' SECONDS
    ) AS cur
    ON t.currency = cur.currency_code

docs.title: Snapshot query
docs.text:
dbt supports running materialized tables and streaming tables. The Confluent REST API exposes a "run Flink statement" operation that can also be used for snapshot queries. The backend application uses the confluent-sql module to demonstrate the integration inside a human-facing dashboard.

See this Confluent client code, which can be summarized as getting a connection using environment variables like the compute pool dedicated for snapshot queries:

s = self._settings
try:
    conn = confluent_sql.connect(
        organization_id=s.FLINK_ORG_ID,
        environment_id=s.FLINK_ENV_ID,
        cloud_provider=s.CLOUD_PROVIDER,
        cloud_region=s.CLOUD_REGION,
        compute_pool_id=s.FLINK_SNAPSHOT_COMPUTE_POOL_ID,
        flink_api_key=s.FLINK_API_KEY,
        flink_api_secret=s.FLINK_API_SECRET,
        database=s.FLINK_DATABASE,
        database_kafka_cluster_id=s.KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID,
    )
    ...
    cur = conn.cursor()  # snapshot mode is the default
    cur.execute(sql)
    columns = [d[0] for d in (cur.description or [])]

docs.title: Lightning query
docs.text:
The Confluent Cloud Real-Time Context Engine (RTCE) exposes a Flink-maintained table for current-state point lookups over HTTP: a single synchronous POST returns the table's current rows in milliseconds.

The request uses HTTP Basic auth with a dedicated Global resource API key (CONFLUENT_GLOBAL_KEY/SECRET, provisioned by IaC/ccloud/lightning.tf) and a body scoped by catalog_name = environment ID and database_name = Kafka cluster ID (IDs, not the display names that the Flink SQL Statements API uses).

See the HTTP client code reference.

Chat with the Real-Time Context Engine

docs.title: Interactive data science with Jupyter Notebooks & Lightning queries
docs.text:
Data scientists and ML engineers can perform exploratory data analysis and feature extraction directly against the real-time Streamhouse state without waiting for batch ETL or staging database copies. By executing HTTP queries against Confluent Cloud's Lightning Query API (Real-Time Context Engine), results from golden record fact tables (like fct_c360_profile) return in milliseconds directly into Python pandas.DataFrame structures.

A ready-to-run notebook is provided at notebooks/c360_profile_lightning_query.ipynb, illustrating: - Sub-second (< 300 ms) point lookups by customer primary key. - Customer segment analysis (e.g. SMB vs. PRIVATE average balances and transaction volumes). - Direct bridge between streaming state and Python data science / AI workflows.

See the demonstration script for how to run the notebook.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The generic application behavior is:

  • Microservice applications write to database tables.
  • A PostgreSQL database server hosts the tables.
  • The Debezium CDC Kafka connector creates one topic per table and defines the schemas in Schema Registry.
  • A set of Flink queries prepares the data to build Customer 360 analytics metrics, which are served in sink topics.
  • Sink topics are processed by Tableflow to export data as Iceberg tables / Parquet files into object storage.
  • External catalogs are kept in sync with the Tableflow catalog.
  • A web application supports demonstrating Streamhouse capabilities.

Two architectures are presented in this repository: one purely in the cloud, and one hybrid with a local server, database, and CDC feeding the Confluent Cloud Kafka cluster and Streamhouse:

Hybrid cloudCloud VPC to VPC

This is the simplest deployment: the database and code run locally, with Confluent Cloud providing Kafka, Flink, Tableflow, and Streamhouse components.

Local Database - Confluent Cloud Streamhouse

  • The PostgreSQL server runs locally in a container (on Mac; Docker Compose on Windows is not yet supported).
  • A Kafka Connect Debezium container image runs locally to capture changes from the 3 tables into the cdc.public.* topics.
  • The web app runs locally.

The web app provides simple navigation to create, update, and delete customers and accounts. Transactions can only be created.

Application Customers Page

The end-to-end, more complex architecture looks like the following figure:

Cloud Deployment - Confluent Cloud Streamhouse

  • The application runs on an EC2 host.
  • The PostgreSQL database server runs on AWS RDS.
  • The Debezium CDC Kafka connector is deployed as a managed service.
  • The Kafka cluster, Schema Registry, Real-Time Context Engine, Tableflow, and Flink jobs run on Confluent Cloud.

Note

Because it is more complex to deploy, this architecture is still under construction and testing.

docs.text:
The Streamhouse architecture offers services for three different actors:

  1. Site Reliability Engineer (SRE)
  2. Data Engineer
  3. Application Developer

docs.title: SRE
docs.text:
This use case demonstrates the tasks an SRE needs to perform to prepare an environment that supports the architecture above.

There are two ways to execute those tasks: via the Confluent Cloud Console, or via infrastructure as code using Terraform. The following bullet points are generic task descriptions that apply to both approaches (some are for production deployment only).

  1. Create the Confluent Cloud environment, API keys and secrets, service accounts, role bindings, and Kafka cluster.
  2. For production deployment, create a private network and a network link to Confluent Cloud.
  3. Create a Schema Registry for a given environment.
  4. Create a Flink compute pool.
  5. Create source databases, for example, an RDS service with a PostgreSQL instance.
  6. Create the Debezium CDC source connector for the database tables using Terraform.
  7. Create the SQL tables in the selected PostgreSQL database: accounts, customers, and transactions.

This list will be updated as this demonstration is implemented.

docs.title: Data Engineer
docs.text:
The following steps are generic and may be supported by different tools:

  1. Create a dbt project to manage Flink statements in a git repository. One approach is to use the star schema (see the note below).
  2. Develop Flink queries using Confluent Cloud Workspace cells.
  3. Save queries to files in the git repository and transform them for dbt.
  4. Deploy the Flink logic using the dbt CLI: dbt run.

This list will be updated as this demonstration is implemented.

We recommend organizing the Flink statements using the star model, a multidimensional data model used to organize data in a data warehouse. It denormalizes business data into dimensions and facts. The fact table sits at the center of the star schema and records what happened, as quantitative, measurable events. The dimension tables (the "context") surround the fact table and provide the who, what, where, when, and why.

docs.title: Application Developer
docs.text:
The following steps are generic and may be supported by different tools:

  1. Define the contract for data and analytics, and the methodology for engaging with data engineers as part of the microservice design.
  2. Maintain schema evolution with full transitivity.
  3. Integrate data in Kafka via Lightning queries or snapshot queries.

This list will be updated as this demonstration is implemented.

  • The web app, delivered as an MVP, illustrates the integration of these new query capabilities to serve data to applications.

This section addresses the Flink pipeline definition and management using Confluent dbt plugin.

docs.title: What is built
docs.text:
We want to implement the following pipeline to process the raw/bronze layer of records coming out of the CDC Debezium source kafka connector (cdc.*):

To a silver layer which includes clean source data, with no duplicate, reflecting a canonical model and filtered records. The golden layer includes the star schema dimensions and facts. For this demonstration the c360-profile defines analytics about a customer based on the buying transactions done so far.

The Confluent Cloud Flink statement organization reflects the medallion and star schema structure. The Flink statements run in a compute pool already created via the Terraform deployment (or reused and referenced in FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID).

  1. First, create the pipeline folder to manage the different Flink SQL statements, using the star schema pattern. This can be done manually or using a tool from flink-tools-for-agents project, which complement the dbt Confluent CLI: 

    git clone https://github.com/jbcodeforce/flink-tools-for-agents.git
cd flink-tools-for-agents
# run shift left for dbt project
uv run sl-dbt init ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo

    Here is the expected structure: 

    streamhouse_c360_demo
├── docs
├── IaC
├── local-tests
├── pipelines
├── sl_dbt.yaml
└── tools

  2. Add a data analytic product named c360, to keep metrics for the Customer 360 view. 

    uv run sl-dbt add-data-product ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo c360

    Here is the expected structure: 

    pipelines
    ├── dbt_project.yml
    ├── macros
    ├── models
    │   └── c360
    │       ├── dimensions
    │       ├── facts
    │       └── sources
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── seeds
    └── tests

  3. Add one table as output of deduplicating raw customer data and filtering unnecessary records:

     uv run sl-dbt add-table ~/Code/streamhouse_c360_demo src_customers c360 --table-type  src

    pipelines
    ├── dbt_project.yml
    ├── macros
    ├── models
    │   └── c360
    │       ├── dimensions
    │       ├── facts
    │       ├── schema.yml
    │       └── sources
    │           ├── src_customers.sql
    │           └── src_customers.yml
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── seeds
    └── tests

  4. Use the Confluent Cloud Workspace to develop query by using an incremental approach: starts by selecting the different sources, to assess data quality. We will illustrate the approach for beginner.

    1. Assess the source table structure. Run the SQL: show create table cdc.public.customers

      We can observe that the Debezium envelope is already transformed to the sub-schema. We can verify the schema definition in Schema Registry has a before and after envelope. Go to the Schema Registry page and select cdc.public.customers-value. The schema has Debezium fields: before, after, op...

      The reason is the default format for the value and the key are set as: 

      value.format' = 'avro-debezium-registry'
      which means the Kafka Source connector inside Confluent Cloud Flink uses a specific deserializer that processes the envelop model.

      We can do the same for: show create table cdc.public.accounts; and show create table cdc.public.transactions;

      We can also discover that by default the changelog mode is set to retract. This is due to the CDC Debezium configuration that may not have defined the primary key mapping. If the Kafka topic has cleanup.policy set to compact, the changelog.mode is set to upsert instead. With retract mode we cannot run snapshot queries, only streaming queries.

    2. Look at some data and select only active customers: 

      SELECT * FROM `j9r-env`.`j9r-kafka`.`cdc.public.customers` where status = 'ACTIVE';

    3. Because the changelog mode is retract or upsert, within the topic there will be no duplicate for the current customers, accounts and transactions, the following query helps to validate that: 

       with deduped_customer as (
    SELECT 
            customer_id,
        FROM `cdc.public.customers`
    ),
    numdup as (SELECT
        customer_id,
        count(*) as num_records
    FROM deduped_customer
    group by customer_id)
    select * from numdup where num_records > 1

  5. We can continue the data analysis and finally build the following Flink SQL for filtering and data cleaning. See the Flink source processing folder.

  6. To be able to connect to Confluent Cloud, we need to set the environment variables for API keys and secrets. The following script loads those from Terraform output 

    source ./scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh

    Alternatively, source the .env file under apps/backend/.

  7. dbt needs models. The first layer is the references to existing CDC topics see pipelines/models/sources.yaml file.

    version: 2
sources:
- name: cdc
schema: "{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME') }}"
tables:
- name: customers
    identifier: cdc.public.customers
- name: accounts
    identifier: cdc.public.accounts
    description: accounts information for a customer    
- name: transactions
    identifier: cdc.public.transactions
    description: Topic 'cdc.public.transactions' — registered via sl-dbt get-schema-existing-topic-to-dbt.

  8. Be sure to modify your .dbt/profiles.yml with the following element. 

    cc_flink:
    outputs:
        dev:
            cloud_provider: '{{ env_var(''CC_PROVIDER'') }}'
            cloud_region: '{{ env_var('CC_REGION'') }}'
            compute_pool_id: '{{ env_var('FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID'') }}'
            dbname: '{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME'') }}'
            environment_id: '{{ env_var('ENVIRONMENT_ID'') }}'
            execution_mode: streaming_query
            flink_api_key: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_KEY'') }}'
            flink_api_secret: '{{ env_var(''FLINK_API_SECRET'') }}'
            organization_id: '{{ env_var(''CC_ORG_ID'') }}'
            statement_label: dbt-confluent
            statement_name_prefix: dbt-
            threads: 4
            type: confluent
    target: dev

    This is a generic profile for Confluent Cloud that uses environment variables to avoid sharing secrets in yaml file.

  9. Continue to create the following Flink statements to filter and transform raw CDC topics, and create dimensions and facts for the analytics.

The path is pipelines/models/c360

Source Table(s) Folder Name Sink Table Goal cdc.public.accounts sources src_accounts Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.customers sources src_customers Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform cdc.public.transactions sources src_transactions Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_customers dimension dim_customers Compute customer dimension src_customers, src_account dimension dim_customers Compute transaction cross account metrics dim_customers, facts fct_c360_profiles 
├── c360
│   ├── dimensions
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.sql
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.yml
│   │   ├── dim_customers.sql
│   │   ├── dim_customers.yml
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.sql
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.yml
│   │   ├── dim_tx_x_account.sql
│   │   └── dim_tx_x_account.yml
│   ├── facts
│   │   └── fct_c360_profile.sql
│   └── sources
│       ├── src_accounts.sql
│       ├── src_accounts.yml
│       ├── src_customers.sql
│       ├── src_customers.yml
│       ├── src_transactions.sql
│       └── src_transactions.yml
├── deploy_manifest.json
└── sources.yaml

Each model needs to have the table definition to create as a sink. As an example, the dimension to compute account aggregations looks like this (dim_account_tx_agg.sql):

models:
- name: dim_account_tx_agg
  description: "Aggregates cross account"
  config:
    contract:
      enforced: true
  columns:
  - name: account_id
    data_type: varchar(2147483647)
    constraints:
      - type: not_null
      - type: primary_key
        expression: "not enforced"
  - name: customer_id
    data_type: string
  - name: account_type
    data_type: string
  - name: account_status
    data_type: string
  - name: balance
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_count
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_total
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: last_transacted_at
    data_type: timestamp_ltz

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
dbt supports different ways to manage dependencies. We can use tags, folders, or the dependency tree.

  • Deploy all the sources that are the first level of flink statements to deploy 
    # within the pipelines folder:
dbt run --select c360.sources --full-refresh
  • Deploy the facts and its parents
# within the pipelines folder:
dbt run --select +c360.facts.fct_c360_profile
# Deploy other product

docs.title: RDS out of storage - connection from client rejected
docs.text:
When an AWS RDS PostgreSQL instance reaches a storage-full state, AWS restricts database access and rejects standard client connections to prevent corruption.

Even without new application data being inserted, PostgreSQL can rapidly fill disk space through Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) retention, abandoned replication slots, verbose error logging, or orphaned temp files.

  • Need to scale up storage, max storage limit and current storage by +20%.

  • Connect with psql (be sure your public IP address is in the security group policy as inbound rules on port 5432) 

    export RDSHOST="c360-j9r-postgres.c......rds.amazonaws.com" 
psql "host=$RDSHOST port=5432 dbname=c360db user=dbadmin sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=~/.ssh/global-bundle.pem"

  • Identify why storage growth occurred. Once connected via psql or your SQL client, run the following diagnostic checks. First, check for abandoned or inactive replication slots (most common cause): if you have an inactive read replica or a disconnected CDC tool (AWS DMS, Debezium, Kafka), PostgreSQL will indefinitely hold Write-Ahead Logs (WAL) on disk waiting for the consumer to catch up. 

    SELECT slot_name, plugin, active, 
    pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS wal_lag
FROM pg_replication_slots;

  • If a slot has active = false and high wal_lag, drop the slot to immediately clear accumulated WAL files: 

    SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('your_slot_name');

  • Check for long-running or stuck transactions: Uncommitted or long-running transactions prevent PostgreSQL from vacuuming dead tuples and clearing old WAL files. 

    SELECT pid, age(clock_timestamp(), query_start), usename, state, query 
FROM pg_stat_activity 
WHERE state != 'idle' 
ORDER BY query_start ASC;

  • Inspect RDS log file accumulation: Verbose error logging (e.g., repeated connection failure loops or heavy query logging) can generate tens of gigabytes of text log files on the host. Go to RDS Console > Databases > [Your Instance] > Logs & events.

    • If log files are taking up massive space, check your DB Parameter Group and adjust rds.log_retention_period to a shorter duration (e.g., 1440 minutes / 1 day).
    • log_min_duration_statement: Increase this value (e.g., 5000 for 5 seconds) or set it to -1 to disable slow query logging entirely.
    • log_statement: Change to none or ddl (avoid all)
    • log_min_messages: Set to warning or error (avoid info or debug).
    • log_parameter_max_length: Reduce this value (e.g., 1024) to cap the size of logged query bind parameters

  • Check for file bloat: complex queries (e.g., large sorts or joins exceeding work_mem) create temp files on disk. Aborted operations can sometimes leave orphaned temp files. 

    SELECT datname, temp_files, pg_size_pretty(temp_bytes) AS temp_size 
FROM pg_stat_database;

docs.title: Streamhouse on Confluent Platform
docs.text:
Version

Last updated: 2026-11-24

This note assesses what needs to be done to run a Streamhouse on top of Confluent Platform. Streamhouse can be implemented on top of self-managed products, for air-gapped and hybrid cloud architectures.

docs.title: Streamhouse Capabilities Mapped to CP
docs.text:
With a self-managed platform, some Streamhouse capabilities need to be stitched together by architects and SREs.

  • Capture: Ingest real-time database changes or operational events with Kafka connectors (100+ connectors), and Flink CDC directly from databases. In Confluent Platform, connector configuration is done via Kubernetes custom resources. CP Flink supports CDC, JDBC, and Filesystem connectors.
  • Transport: Buffer and retain event streams with a Confluent Platform Kafka cluster.
  • Transform: Run stateful stream processing, enrichments, or windowed aggregations via Flink SQL, Table API, Python Flink (PyFlink) or DataStream API. See Confluent platform for Apache Flink documentation
  • Store (Lakehouse Sink): Persist continuously updated streams into open table formats like Apache Iceberg backed by object storage (e.g., MinIO or S3).
  • Serve: Query unified batch and streaming data layers with low-latency engines like Trino. Apache Flink connectors are supported.

  • Apache Flink Iceberg Sink Connector enables Apache Flink applications to write batch and real-time streaming data directly into Apache Iceberg tables with ACID guarantees and exactly-once semantics. It is distributed as part of the iceberg-flink-runtime dependency and supports both Flink SQL and the Java DataStream API.

  • Governance is supported by Schema Registry and the Unified Stream Manager, which integrates self-managed Confluent Platform clusters and self-managed Connect clusters with Confluent Cloud to provide a single user interface and sets Confluent Cloud as the authoritative control plane for governance tasks, while on-premises Confluent Platform continues to serve as the data plane.

docs.title: CP Capabilities
docs.text:
• Flink Job Manager orchestration done by Kubernetes - Task managers done by Job Manager.
  • The time series analytics model deployed on Confluent Cloud, are the same running as pods inside Confluent Platform
  • SQL batch queries are analog to snapshot queries.
  • Chatbook, a natural language SQL notebook
  • Confluent Private Cloud
  • Confluent Gateway

docs.text:
• K-serve platform designed to standardize, scale, and manage machine learning (ML) model inference in production, on kubernetes. It uses the InferenceService Custom Resource to specify your model, runtime, and scaling options

docs.text:

  • Plan authentication, authorization, and network encryption.
  • Plan Capacity and Sizing for Confluent for Kubernetes: Size CPU, memory, and storage for deployed workload.
  • Plan log retention and review configuration constraints.
  • Establish query on the index, using software like Redis, or Cassandra

The Analytics page illustrates what can be done by directly accessing data in Kafka.

Rather than pulling every customer row and folding it in the backend, the cross-customer aggregates are built in Flink as a CRM analytic data product — four small materialized tables ( fct_crm_by_segment, fct_crm_by_generation, fct_crm_by_gender, fct_crm_by_country) derived from dim_customers, plus the fact tables fct_crm_summary, and fct_c360_profile. docs.title: Fit for Purpose
docs.text:
Version

Last updated: 2026-11-24

Once the Flink pipeline has materialized fct_c360_profile (and the CRM data products) in Kafka, there are several ways to read that data back, and one way to act on it continuously. They look similar from the outside (SQL in, rows out), but they are built for different jobs. This page helps a solution engineer pick the right one, and explains what to say when a customer asks "why not just use X?".

Need Use Demo page Serve one customer's current state to an app or an AI agent, in well under a second, from many concurrent clients Lightning query (Lightning Tables, served by the Real-Time Context Engine) Lightning widget, Assistant chat Run an ad-hoc, analytical query (aggregations, joins, sorting) over a topic, once, and get a consistent answer Flink snapshot query Snapshot widget, analytics dashboard Continuously compute, enrich or react to events as they arrive Flink streaming statement (the dbt pipeline) Statement graph Let an LLM reason and call tools on each event, inside the stream Streaming Agents (CREATE AGENT + AI_RUN_AGENT) (not in the demo yet)

Sources

Facts below come from the Confluent Cloud documentation (Lightning Tables, Query a Lightning Table, Real-Time Context Engine, Snapshot Queries, Streaming Agents) and from what this demo's backend does. Lightning Tables and the Real-Time Context Engine are recent, fast-moving features: re-check limits, regions and pricing before quoting them.

docs.title: The three query modes in one picture
docs.text:
The Confluent documentation compares them directly:

Lightning query Snapshot query Streaming query How it runs Runs once, returns in less than a second Runs once, returns results, exits Runs continuously, returns results incrementally Engine Managed table optimized for lookups, no Flink job A Flink job in batch mode A Flink job in streaming mode Best for Point lookups, range scans, full scans from many concurrent clients such as applications and AI agents. Select using primary key as index. Complex, exploratory analysis over historical data Processing data continuously as it arrives Cost model Usage-based: compute (CCU minutes), bytes scanned, storage CFUs, same as streaming CFUs while running

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A Lightning Table is a managed materialization of a Kafka topic, optimized for fast lookups. You enable it per topic (Console, CLI, terraform or API). Confluent Cloud keeps it updated within 100 ms of new data arriving, with no consumers to write and no Flink job to run. The Real-Time Context Engine (RTCE) is the MCP (Model Context Protocol) interface to those same tables.

A Lightning query is read-only SQL on a single table, reachable through five interfaces that all read the same table:

Interface Auth Typical client Console User login Exploration HTTP API (https://sql.<region>.<cloud>.confluent.cloud/query/v1) Global API key (Basic) Applications, dashboards, services (this demo's lightning_client.py) MCP (RTCE) Global API key, Confluent sign-in or OAuth AI agents (this demo's Assistant) Confluent CLI (confluent lightning query) User login Scripts JDBC Global API key BI tools, Java apps

docs.title: Choose it when
docs.text:
• The consumer is an operational application or an AI agent that needs the current state of one entity ("what is customer Carter's balance and segment right now?"), repeatedly and concurrently.
  • Latency is a requirement, not a nice-to-have. A snapshot query spins up a Flink job each time; a Lightning query does not.
  • You do not want to run infrastructure: no compute pool sizing, no cache, no serving database in front of Kafka.
  • The reader should not know Kafka: a business user or an LLM asks for data and gets rows. The RTCE exposes exactly three MCP tools, listTopics, getMetadata and queryData, and the documented agent workflow is discover, inspect, then query.
  • You need data that has aged out of the topic. A Lightning Table persists independently of the topic's retention policy, so it can return records that Kafka has already deleted.

docs.title: Be careful when
docs.text: Constraint Detail Single-table, read-only SQL Supports key lookups, WHERE filters (=, !=, <, IN, LIKE, BETWEEN, IS NULL, AND/OR), column selection, ORDER BY and LIMIT. No aggregates (COUNT, SUM...), GROUP BY, joins, subqueries, set operators, DDL or DML. Result size and time Over MCP: at most 200 rows and a 20 s timeout; max_result_rows is mandatory on every queryData call; rate limiting returns RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. The HTTP API returns small results inline (200) and large or slow ones asynchronously (202 plus a statement ID to poll). Different data than Flink may see A Lightning query reads the table, not the topic, so it "might return different results than a Flink streaming or snapshot query on the same topic". Do not use it to reconcile against Flink output. Topic prerequisites Needs a registered schema (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) and a Kafka record key, which the table uses as its primary key for deduplication. The key schema cannot change afterwards. Upsert vs append Mode follows cleanup.policy. compact plus a record key gives upsert (latest row per key, tombstones delete); delete gives append (all records). For "current profile per customer", you want upsert. Schema evolution Supported changes keep working; an unsupported one (for example a renamed column or a changed key schema) stops ingestion until you revert or move to a new topic. Credentials A Global API key (organization-wide). Cluster-, environment- or Flink-scoped keys return 401, which is why lightning_client.py calls this out. Also needs DeveloperRead on the topic and the Schema Registry cluster. Private networking Console and CLI queries do not work over private networking. Use API, MCP or JDBC through a private endpoint.

docs.title: In this demo
docs.text:
• fct_c360_profile is the table behind the Lightning widget. The backend calls the HTTP API from analytics/lightning_client.py with a Global key, catalog_name = environment ID and database_name = cluster ID. It is best-effort: missing credentials or a non-2xx answer yield no rows rather than an exception.
  • The Assistant chat uses the RTCE MCP endpoint through an Agno agent, to show a business user asking a question in natural language and getting live Kafka data, with no pipeline code in between.

Talk track

"Flink did the hard work once, continuously: it joined, deduplicated and aggregated into one profile row per customer. Lightning makes that row servable: the app or the agent asks, and gets an answer in milliseconds. Same Kafka topic, no cache, no extra database."

docs.title: When to use Flink Snapshot Query
What it is
docs.text:
A snapshot query is an ordinary Flink SQL statement with one extra property, sql.snapshot.mode = 'now'. Flink switches to batch mode, bounds every input at the current moment (AS OF NOW()), computes the result, releases its resources and exits. You cannot query an arbitrary past point in time yet. It works on Kafka topics, including ones with Tableflow enabled, but not on Iceberg or Delta tables that Tableflow write.

It can be launched from the Console (the Mode dropdown), SQL (SET 'sql.snapshot.mode' = 'now';), the REST Statements API (spec.properties), Terraform, the Table API, or confluent flink query (which sets the property for you).

docs.title: Choose it when
docs.text:
• The question needs the full SQL engine: GROUP BY, joins across topics, window or analytic functions, global ORDER BY. Batch mode enables global sorting, blocking operators and efficient joins that streaming cannot offer.
  • You are exploring a new dataset before committing to a streaming pipeline, or debugging ("what does the data look like right now?").
  • You need a consistent, deterministic answer: the default isolation level is read-committed, aligned with Kafka exactly-once semantics, so results are free of partial or aborted writes, and rerunning on the same data gives the same result.
  • You want reports, audits or reconciliations against what is actually in the topic.
  • A handful of callers, an occasional call, where a few seconds of latency is acceptable. The demo's analytics dashboard fits: five trivial SELECT * on pre-aggregated fct_crm_* tables, run concurrently, with the aggregation already done in Flink.

docs.title: Be careful when
docs.text: Constraint Detail Latency Each query is a statement submitted to a compute pool, so it pays job start-up and result polling. Expect seconds rather than milliseconds (measure it in your own environment, the docs give no figure). Concurrency Every call consumes compute (billed in CFUs, like streaming). It is not a serving layer for thousands of simultaneous users. Not a pipeline It runs once and exits. If the result must stay current, use a streaming statement writing to a topic, then read that topic. A plain SELECT needs a consumer Via statement create (without confluent flink query or the SQL driver fetching rows), nothing reads the result and Confluent Cloud stops the statement after five minutes.

docs.title: In this demo
docs.text:
• The Snapshot widget and the analytics dashboard run snapshot queries through the confluent-sql DB-API driver (analytics/confluent_sql_client.py, analytics/crm_provider.py).
  • Putting the aggregation in Flink (fct_crm_*) and doing only SELECT * at read time is deliberate: do the heavy lifting in the stream, keep the read trivial. That is also what makes the Lightning variant possible, because Lightning cannot aggregate.

Talk track

"Snapshot is for the analyst and the engineer: full Flink SQL, consistent, pay for what you run. Lightning is for the app and the AI agent: one row, fast, many callers. Use the first to understand the data, the second to serve it."

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
Question Lightning Snapshot Latency target Sub-second Seconds Many concurrent callers Designed for it Poor fit (one Flink job per call) Aggregations, joins at read time No Yes Data aged out of retention Yes No (reads the topic) Result size Small (200 rows over MCP) Large possible Runs infrastructure you size No Compute pool (CFUs) Natural client App, AI agent, BI via JDBC Analyst, notebook, batch job Failure mode to know Unsupported schema change halts ingestion Statement stopped if nothing consumes the result

Rule of thumb: model with Flink streaming so each topic already holds the shape the reader wants (one row per key, pre-aggregated). Then serve that topic with Lightning, and keep snapshot for the questions you did not model in advance.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Streaming Agents (part of Confluent Intelligence) are event-driven AI agents that run inside Flink SQL, on the data stream, instead of beside it. Everything is a first-class SQL resource:

-- 1. The tool: an MCP server or a Flink UDF
CREATE CONNECTION tx_mcp
WITH ('type' = 'mcp_server', 'endpoint' = '<tx-mcp-url>', 'api-key' = '<key>');

CREATE TOOL tx_tool USING CONNECTION tx_mcp
WITH ('type' = 'mcp', 'allowed_tools' = 'queryData,getMetadata', 'request_timeout' = '30');

-- 2. The agent: model + prompt + tools
CREATE AGENT tx_review_agent
  USING MODEL my_llm
  USING PROMPT 'You review a flagged card transaction. Look up the customer profile, decide APPROVE / REVIEW / BLOCK and explain briefly.'
  USING TOOLS tx_tool
  WITH ('max_iterations' = '5');

-- 3. Run it on every event
SELECT tx_id, response
FROM flagged_transactions,
LATERAL TABLE(AI_RUN_AGENT('tx_review_agent', `message`, `tx_id`, 'agent_system_table'));

Key building blocks, from the documentation:

Capability What it gives you Function call agent Declarative agent: role (prompt), capabilities (tools), model. The runtime runs the reason-and-act loop (max_iterations, default 20; max_consecutive_failures, default 3). Tools CREATE TOOL over a Flink UDF (runs locally in Flink, lowest latency) or an MCP / A2A server (external services). allowed_tools restricts what the agent may call. Models Any model you register with CREATE MODEL / CREATE CONNECTION: OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, AWS SageMaker, Google Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry. Reflection workflows A drafter agent and a critic agent loop until the critic approves (pass_condition of approval or confidence) or the iteration limit is hit. Context management Token strategies none, trim or summarize when a conversation exceeds max_tokens_threshold. Observability & replay A system log table captures every chat message, model response, tool call and error; replay lets you test a new agent version against history without side effects. Console Create and manage agents without writing SQL.

docs.title: Choose it when
docs.text:
• The trigger is an event, not a person typing. The agent fires for every flagged transaction, support ticket or sensor reading.
  • The decision needs judgment over context that a rule or MATCH_RECOGNIZE pattern cannot encode: free text, ambiguous signals, multi-step lookups.
  • The result belongs back in the stream: the agent's output is a new row/topic that downstream statements, Tableflow or applications consume.
  • You want governance and auditability of AI behavior (traceable tool calls, replay) rather than ad-hoc scripts.

docs.title: Use cases (and how they map to this demo)
docs.text:
Use case Event that triggers the agent Context the agent fetches Output Fraud triage A row from fct_fraud_probe, fct_merchant_streak or fct_smb_spike (the MATCH_RECOGNIZE models) Customer profile from fct_c360_profile through RTCE/Lightning. Recent history Verdict (approve / review / block), rationale, recommended action Next-best-action / personalization A change to a customer's segment, balance or activity in fct_c360_profile Profile, product catalogue (MCP or external table) Tailored message or offer, written to a topic for the CRM Customer-service automation A new support ticket or chat message Account lookup tool (UDF), ticket system (MCP) Draft reply, routing decision, ticket creation Data-quality stewardship A customer record that fails validation rules (illustrative, not in the pipeline today) Related rows, reference rules Corrected record or exception ticket IoT / predictive maintenance Sensor window breaching a threshold Equipment history Maintenance work order Content moderation / enrichment New user-generated text Policy documents Category, severity, AI_SENTIMENT style tags Compliance review High-value or unusual transfer Customer risk profile Case summary for an analyst, using a reflection agent for quality

The pattern that ties it together in this repository: Flink CEP detects, Lightning/RTCE supplies fresh context, the Streaming Agent decides. That is the "art of the possible" story in three layers, all on one Streamhouse platform.

docs.title: Be careful when
docs.text:
• Do not use an agent where deterministic SQL is enough. A rule such as "amount > 5000 and new merchant" is cheaper, faster and reproducible as a Flink statement. Use the agent for the residual ambiguous cases, after the cheap filter.
  • LLM calls are slow and billed per token. Throughput of an agent statement is bounded by model latency and rate limits; filter upstream so only the interesting events reach AI_RUN_AGENT, and size max_iterations and request_timeout to the task (a chatbot needs seconds; a research agent minutes).
  • Make tools idempotent. The runtime retries (with exponential back-off for rate limits), so a tool that creates a ticket must tolerate being called twice.
  • Prefer UDF tools for high-frequency calls, MCP tools for external systems.
  • Mind the data path of the context. An agent that queries the RTCE through queryData gets at most 200 rows and 20 s per call, so give it narrow, key-based questions, not scans.
  • Treat prompts and tool inputs as untrusted. Restrict allowed_tools, keep API keys in connections, and review the system log table.
  • Maturity: Streaming Agents and Lightning Tables are new Confluent Intelligence capabilities; syntax and limits are still evolving. The statement graph and the dbt pipeline already cover the deterministic path, so position agents as the next layer, not a replacement.

docs.title: Flink Project Management with dbt
docs.text:
Version

Last updated: 2026-11-24

This section describes how the different Flink pipelines are defined, deployed and removed with the Confluent dbt plugin. The dbt project is in the pipelines/ folder.

As of 11/24* all commands were performed on MacOS.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Be sure to get the last version of Confluent dbt, getting from PyPi: adapt the version in pipelines/pyproject.toml 

      dependencies = [
  "dbt-confluent>=0.6.0"
  ]

  2. Start virtual environment to run dbt 

    cd pipelines
source .venv/bin/activate
# if new version was specified
uv sync

  3. To connect to Confluent Cloud, dbt needs the API keys, secrets and ids as environment variables. This script loads them from the Terraform outputs (see Defining Confluent Cloud Resources with Terraform):

    # still in pipelines
source ../scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh

    As an alternative, load the apps/backend/.env file that the script writes:

    set -a; source apps/backend/.env; set +a

    Verify the settings via: 

    printenv

  4. Normally on brand new project, dbt init is run. See Confluent dbt documentation. Init build also a $HOME/.dbt/profiles.yml file that includes references to Confluent cloud environment (or other dbt backend).

  5. Add the profile below to ~/.dbt/profiles.yml. As of now, the profile name must be j9r, to match the value set as profile in dbt_project.yml. Align names if you change. The below declartion, for dbt to read everything from environment variables, so no secret is stored in the file:

    j9r:
  outputs:
    dev:
      cloud_provider: "{{ env_var('CLOUD_PROVIDER') }}"
      cloud_region: "{{ env_var('CLOUD_REGION') }}"
      compute_pool_id: "{{ env_var('FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID') }}"
      dbname: "{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME') }}"
      environment_id: "{{ env_var('FLINK_ENV_ID') }}"
      execution_mode: streaming_query
      flink_api_key: "{{ env_var('FLINK_API_KEY') }}"
      flink_api_secret: "{{ env_var('FLINK_API_SECRET') }}"
      organization_id: "<your-confluent-organization-id>"
      statement_label: dbt-confluent
      statement_name_prefix: dbt-
      threads: 4
      type: confluent
  target: dev

    The set_env_from_tf.sh does not export the organization id. Get it from the Confluent Console, or with confluent organization list.

    The compute_pool_id of the profile is overridden per data product in dbt_project.yml: c360 models run on FLINK_COMPUTE_POOL_ID and crm adnfraud models run on FLINK_CRM_COMPUTE_POOL_ID. This lets the Cost API attribute to present the cost per product.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The first layer of models references the existing CDC topics, declared in pipelines/models/sources.yaml:

version: 2
sources:
- name: cdc
  schema: "{{ env_var('KAFKA_CLUSTER_NAME') }}"
  tables:
  - name: customers
    identifier: cdc.public.customers
  - name: accounts
    identifier: cdc.public.accounts
    description: accounts information for a customer
  - name: transactions
    identifier: cdc.public.transactions
    description: Topic 'cdc.public.transactions'.
  - name: cards
    identifier: cdc.public.cards
    description: Topic 'cdc.public.cards'.
  • Important to note that the database name for the schema entry, is defined as Kafka cluster name.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
The models are organized by data product under pipelines/models: c360, crm and fraud. Each product has a sources, dimensions and facts folder, and each model has a .sql file and a .yml file. Models are linked with ref(), so a model can depend on a model of another product: the c360 dimensions use src_accounts and dim_customers from crm.

models
├── c360
│   ├── dimensions
│   │   ├── dim_account_tx_agg.{sql,yml}
│   │   ├── dim_transactions.{sql,yml}
│   │   └── dim_tx_x_account.{sql,yml}
│   ├── facts
│   │   ├── fct_c360_profile.{sql,yml}
│   │   ├── fct_crm_summary.{sql,yml}
│   │   ├── fct_hourly_tx_metrics.{sql,yml}
│   │   └── fct_merchant_streak.{sql,yml}
│   └── sources
│       └── src_transactions.{sql,yml}
├── crm
│   ├── dimensions
│   │   └── dim_customers.{sql,yml}
│   ├── facts
│   │   ├── fct_crm_by_country.{sql,yml}
│   │   ├── fct_crm_by_gender.{sql,yml}
│   │   ├── fct_crm_by_generation.{sql,yml}
│   │   └── fct_crm_by_segment.{sql,yml}
│   └── sources
│       ├── src_accounts.{sql,yml}
│       ├── src_cards.{sql,yml}
│       └── src_customers.{sql,yml}
├── fraud
│   └── facts
│       ├── fct_fraud_probe.{sql,yml}
│       └── fct_smb_spike.{sql,yml}
├── deploy_manifest.json
└── sources.yaml
Model Product Inputs Materialization Goal src_transactions c360 cdc.public.transactions streaming table Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_accounts crm cdc.public.accounts streaming table Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_cards crm cdc.public.cards streaming table Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform src_customers crm cdc.public.customers streaming table Deduplicate, flatten, filter, transform dim_customers crm src_accounts, src_cards, src_customers streaming table Customer dimension, with its accounts and cards dim_transactions c360 src_transactions, src_customers, seeds currency_codes and country_codes materialized table Enrich transactions with currency, customer and country dim_account_tx_agg c360 src_accounts, dim_transactions materialized table Transaction aggregates per account dim_tx_x_account c360 dim_customers, dim_account_tx_agg materialized table Transaction and account metrics per customer fct_c360_profile c360 dim_customers, dim_tx_x_account materialized table Customer 360 profile, served by the RTCE Lightning API fct_crm_summary c360 fct_c360_profile materialized table CRM analytics, served by the RTCE Lightning API fct_merchant_streak c360 src_transactions streaming table CEP: three or more consecutive transactions in the same merchant category fct_crm_by_country, _by_gender, _by_generation, _by_segment crm dim_customers materialized table CRM aggregates fct_fraud_probe fraud src_transactions streaming table CEP: small card-test charge followed by large charges fct_smb_spike fraud src_transactions, src_customers streaming table CEP: large debits followed by a credit on an SMB account

Each model needs the definition of the table it creates as sink. As an example, here is the dim_account_tx_agg.yml file of the dimension that computes the account aggregations:

models:
- name: dim_account_tx_agg
  description: "Aggregates cross account"
  config:
    contract:
      enforced: true
  columns:
  - name: account_id
    data_type: varchar(2147483647)
    constraints:
      - type: not_null
      - type: primary_key
        expression: "not enforced"
  - name: customer_id
    data_type: string
  - name: account_type
    data_type: string
  - name: account_status
    data_type: string
  - name: balance
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: txn_count
    data_type: BIGINT
  - name: txn_total
    data_type: DECIMAL
  - name: last_transacted_at
    data_type: timestamp_ltz

To get some tricks and how tos, see this chapter

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
dbt can select the models to deploy by tag, folder or dependency tree. Run the commands from the pipelines folder.

  • Load the reference data (the country_codes (ISO 3166-1 country codes) and currency_codes (ISO 4217 currency codes) seeds), needed by dim_transactions:

    uv run dbt seed

  • Deploy the sources, which are the first level of Flink statements:

    uv run dbt run --select c360.sources crm.sources --full-refresh

  • Deploy a fact table and all its parents:

    uv run dbt run --select +c360.facts.fct_c360_profile

  • Deploy the other products:

    uv run dbt run --select +crm.facts
uv run dbt run --select +fraud.facts

After editing a query, run dbt run --full-refresh on the model to redeploy it. This is required for the CEP models (fct_merchant_streak, fct_fraud_probe, fct_smb_spike).

docs.title: Undeploy
docs.text:
dbt does not support undeploying. The flink-tools-for-agents project provides tools that use a manifest of the existing statements to deploy, undeploy and drop tables. This repository has one in pipelines/models/deploy_manifest.json. It defines:

  • the statement groups c360_pipeline, crm_pipeline and fraud_pipeline, in deploy order;

  • the drop_tables groups c360, crm, fraud, cdc, connect and seeds.

  • Regenerate the manifest if models were added or removed (the clone of flink-tools-for-agents is next to this repository):

    cd flink-tools-for-agents
uv run generate-manifest --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models --overwrite

  • Drop the tables listed in the drop_tables element of the manifest:

    uv run flink-sql-deploy --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models drop-tables --group fraud
uv run flink-sql-deploy --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models drop-tables --group crm
uv run flink-sql-deploy --sql-dir ../streamhouse_c360_demo/pipelines/models drop-tables --group c360

docs.title: Remove the infrastructure
docs.text:
Destroy the Terraform modules in the reverse order of their creation. IaC/ccloud comes last, because IaC/rtce and IaC/connector read its state. Skip the modules you did not apply.

  • Remove the RTCE topics and Global API key:

    cd IaC/rtce && terraform destroy

  • Remove the app host (needs AWS credentials):

    ./scripts/tf_ec2.sh destroy

  • Remove the managed connector:

    ./scripts/tf_connector.sh destroy

  • Remove the AWS resources:

    ./scripts/tf_aws.sh destroy

  • Remove the Confluent Cloud resources:

    cd IaC/ccloud && terraform destroy

For the local PostgreSQL and Debezium containers, see Local CDC.

docs.title: Local CDC: PostgreSQL → Debezium → Confluent Cloud
docs.text:
Version

Last updated: 2026-11-24

Run the CDC path entirely on your workstation: a local PostgreSQL 17 container and a Debezium (Kafka Connect) container publish Avro change events to Confluent Cloud Kafka. This replaces the managed connector in IaC/connector/ and the RDS instance in IaC/AWS/.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• macOS with the Apple container CLI.
  • uv (used by the backend bootstrap).
  • A Confluent Cloud environment (see IaC/ccloud/).

docs.title: 1. Set Confluent Cloud credentials
docs.text:
All variables live in apps/backend/.env (gitignored). Generate it from the Terraform outputs:

./scripts/set_env_from_tf.sh

Debezium needs KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, KAFKA_API_KEY, KAFKA_API_SECRET, SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL, SCHEMA_REGISTRY_API_KEY and SCHEMA_REGISTRY_API_SECRET. Variables already exported in your shell take precedence over the file.

Future execution, when doing new execution from existing Confluent Cloud environment, you just need to set environment variables in the Termincal session with:

set -a && source ./apps/backend/.env && set +a

See also reset data, if you want to restart from new databae and new cdc topics

docs.title: 2. Start the stack
docs.text:
# Start the Apple container runtime
container system start

cd IaC/local

# PostgreSQL 17 with wal_level=logical, plus schema, publication and seed data
./start_local_pg_server.sh --seed
# Alternate start DB server on existing database
./start_local_pg_server.sh
# Debezium worker + connector (waits until the connector is RUNNING)
./start_debezium.sh

--seed runs apps/backend/bootstrap.py, which creates the tables, the c360_cdc_publication publication and the seed data. The Postgres container is already started with wal_level=logical, so no extra CDC configuration step is needed.

Or run both through the dev script: ./scripts/run_dev.sh --cdc.

Verify the containers:

container ls

ID              IMAGE                                  OS     ARCH   STATE    IP                CPUS  MEMORY   STARTED
c360-debezium   quay.io/debezium/connect:3.0.0.Final   linux  arm64  running  192.168.64.66/24  4     2048 MB  2026-11-10T18:10:56Z
c360-postgres   docker.io/library/postgres:17          linux  arm64  running  192.168.64.64/24  4     1024 MB  2026-11-10T17:58:24Z

docs.title: Other platforms (docker compose, untested)
docs.text:
The Apple container CLI does not support docker-compose.yml. On other platforms, IaC/local/ includes a compose file. It has not been tested yet.

cd IaC/local
docker compose --env-file ../../apps/backend/.env up -d --build

# Once Postgres is healthy: create tables, publication and seed data
(cd ../../apps/backend && \
  DATABASE_URL="postgresql://dbadmin:localdevonly@localhost:5432/c360db?sslmode=disable" \
  uv run python bootstrap.py)

docker compose --env-file ../../apps/backend/.env logs -f debezium-connector

docs.title: 3. Verify the pipeline
docs.text:
Kafka topics. Debezium captures the public schema tables listed below. In the Confluent Cloud console, check for the topics:

  • cdc.public.accounts
  • cdc.public.cards
  • cdc.public.customers
  • cdc.public.transactions

Connector status:

curl -s http://localhost:8083/connectors/postgres-cdc/status | jq

PostgreSQL data. Use any PostgreSQL client or IDE plugin (Bob, VS Code, Cursor) on localhost:5432:

docs.title: 4. Stop and reset
docs.text:
cd IaC/local

# Debezium
./start_debezium.sh --stop         # stop and remove the worker
./start_debezium.sh --reset        # recreate the worker (Kafka state kept)
./start_debezium.sh --full-reset   # also wipe Connect topics and drop the replication slot (forces a re-snapshot)

# PostgreSQL
./start_local_pg_server.sh --stop    # stop and remove the container (data is kept)
./start_local_pg_server.sh --purge   # stop and remove the container AND its data volume
./start_local_pg_server.sh --reset   # purge, then start a fresh empty container (data is lost)

docs.title: PostgreSQL data persistence
docs.text:
The PostgreSQL data directory lives on a named volume, c360-pgdata, mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/data with PGDATA=/var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata. The container is disposable; the volume is not.

Action Container Volume c360-pgdata (your data) start_local_pg_server.sh (first run) created created start_local_pg_server.sh (container stopped or removed) restarted or recreated reused, data is back --stop removed kept --purge removed deleted --reset recreated deleted, then recreated empty

Rows you create through the app or SQL therefore survive --stop followed by a restart, a reboot, or an Apple container daemon restart. Only --purge and --reset discard them.

Why this matters: without a volume, PostgreSQL writes to the container's own filesystem, which is destroyed with container delete. Earlier versions of the script had no volume, so --stop/--reset (the latter being the only suggested way out of the "container exists but is not running" error) silently wiped customers created after the initial CSV seed. The seed only reloads the committed CSVs, so those rows were lost.

PGDATA points to a subdirectory because a freshly created volume can contain a lost+found directory, and initdb refuses a non-empty data root.

A container created by an older version of the script has no volume and keeps the old behavior. To migrate, run ./start_local_pg_server.sh --reset --seed once (this loses its current data), or dump it first with pg_dump.

Because the database now survives restarts, the Debezium replication slot and connector offsets stay consistent with it. After --purge or --reset the database is new, so reset Debezium too (see below).

A purged or reset PostgreSQL container is empty: it has no table and no c360_cdc_publication, and start_debezium.sh refuses to start without the publication. Recreate them with --seed, then reset Debezium so the replication slot and offsets match the new database:

./start_local_pg_server.sh --reset --seed
./start_debezium.sh --full-reset

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Set by start_local_pg_server.sh when starting the container:

Setting Value wal_level logical max_wal_senders 4 max_replication_slots 4 Publication c360_cdc_publication (created by the backend bootstrap) Replication slot debezium_slot (created by Debezium)

Optional overrides (defaults shown):

export LOCAL_PG_USER=dbadmin
export LOCAL_PG_PASSWORD=localdevonly
export LOCAL_PG_DB=c360db
export PG_PORT=5432

docs.title: Debezium connector
docs.text:
start_debezium.sh is the single entry point. It checks Postgres, creates the Connect storage topics (my_connect_configs, my_connect_offsets, my_connect_status, replication factor 3), downloads the Confluent Avro converter, starts the c360-debezium worker (REST API on localhost:8083) and applies the postgres-cdc connector with an idempotent PUT /connectors/postgres-cdc/config.

Setting Value Plugin pgoutput Publication c360_cdc_publication (publication.autocreate.mode=disabled) Slot debezium_slot Tables public.accounts, public.cards, public.customers, public.transactions Topic prefix cdc → cdc.public.<table> Format Avro key and value, via Confluent Schema Registry Snapshot snapshot.mode=initial Tombstones tombstones.on.delete=true Topic creation 6 partitions, replication factor 3

The connector reaches Postgres through the container IP (read from container list), not localhost, which inside the Debezium container would be the container itself.

docs.title: Debezium container won't start
docs.text:
(cd IaC/local && ./start_debezium.sh --logs)

Common causes:

  • PostgreSQL is not running: ./start_local_pg_server.sh (restarts a stopped container and keeps its data).
  • wal_level is not logical (container started elsewhere): recreate it with ./start_local_pg_server.sh --reset --seed.
  • Confluent Cloud or Schema Registry credentials are missing from apps/backend/.env and the shell.
  • The publication does not exist: run the backend bootstrap (./start_local_pg_server.sh --seed).

docs.title: No messages in Confluent Cloud
docs.text:
1. Check that the replication slot exists:
container exec c360-postgres psql -U dbadmin -d c360db -c "SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots;"
  1. Check that the publication covers the tables:
container exec c360-postgres psql -U dbadmin -d c360db -c "SELECT * FROM pg_publication_tables WHERE pubname='c360_cdc_publication';"
  1. Check the connector task state (see step 3).

docs.title: Replication slot already exists, or doesn't match
docs.text:
The slot is left over from a previous run, or was created with a different plugin. The connector requires pgoutput. Run ./start_debezium.sh --full-reset, or drop it manually:

container exec c360-postgres psql -U dbadmin -d c360db -c \
  "SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('debezium_slot');"

docs.text: This is mostly due to not enabling it on the fact tables.

This section of the documentation is to create AWS resources for the end-to-end Streamhouse demonstration with source database, S3 buckets and Catalog.

Terraform is organized under the IaC/ directory as three independent root modules (separate local state), each file-per-concern. This split lets the core Confluent Cloud stack run locally with no AWS credentials; AWS and the managed connector are opt-in cost paths.

  • IaC/AWS/ — AWS stack: PostgreSQL RDS 17 (CDC-ready), VPC/subnet lookups, security group (allowlists Confluent egress IPs), KMS, and the Secrets Manager secret consumed by IaC/connector/. Run with scripts/tf_aws.sh, which needs AWS credentials and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY/SECRET exported because the security group setup reads Confluent egress IPs dynamically.

  • IaC/connector/ — managed Debezium Postgres CDC connector on Confluent cloud: reads the core stack's outputs from ../ccloud/terraform.tfstate via terraform_remote_state, and the RDS credentials from AWS Secrets Manager. Run with scripts/tf_connector.sh (needs AWS creds). Optional — in local mode the backend app writes Debezium-shaped events directly to cdc.public.* topics instead.

Apply order: IaC/ccloud → IaC/AWS → IaC/connector.

The resources created are illustrated in the following figure:

  • RDS Postgresql instance
  • Security group and network policies for the application load balancer
  • Secrets

docs.text:

export AWS_PROFILE="your-profile-name"

  • Modify terraform environment variables terraform.tfvars for cloud region, vpc_id and my_ip_addr
  • Be sure to have CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET exported in the Terminal session

docs.title: AWS Resources: RDS Postgresql
docs.text: The database is created in a public subnet of an existing VPC but the security group uses the user ip address to define a rule

docs.title: AWS RDS Postgresql
docs.text:
The terraform under IaC/AWS folder creates the RDS Postgresql 17 instance, with DB subnet group within an existing VPC, security group policies to restrict traffic to PostgreSQL on port 5432 within the existing VPC. The Ingress rules allow access to Postgres TCP port 5432 from VPC, client CIDRs, and Confluent Cloud egress IP addresses.

RDS storage is encrypted with KMS Customer Managed Key and DB secrets. Database credentials are securely saved in AWS Secrets Manager.

Run this stack through the scripts/tf_aws.sh wrapper rather than calling terraform directly. The wrapper handles two credential gotchas that make a bare terraform plan fail:

  • AWS: SSO profiles often store temporary (ASIA…) keys without an aws_session_token in the shared files. The AWS CLI still works from its SSO cache, but Terraform's provider rejects the incomplete set (No valid credential sources found). The wrapper refreshes the SSO token if needed and exports the full key + secret + session-token triple into the environment. It also verifies the resolved account matches the expected one (829250931565 by default; override with EXPECTED_AWS_ACCOUNT_ID) and fails fast if a similarly-named profile lands in the wrong account — e.g. 829250931565_nonprod-administrator actually resolves to 898188061957, so use AWS_PROFILE=default (or another profile in the right account).
  • Confluent: the security group ingress is built from the Confluent Cloud egress IPs, so the Confluent provider needs cloud_api_key / cloud_api_secret. Export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY and CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET before running the wrapper; it defensively strips any incomplete native Schema Registry / Flink env vars that would otherwise trip the provider's all-or-none validation.
# Confluent Cloud API creds must be exported (the wrapper does not read ~/.confluent/.env)
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY=...
export CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_SECRET=...

# Uses the `default` AWS profile unless AWS_PROFILE is set
scripts/tf_aws.sh plan
scripts/tf_aws.sh apply
scripts/tf_aws.sh output

The output gives us the following:

db_security_group_id = "sg-...."
db_subnet_group_name = "c360-j9r-db-subnet-group"
rds_address = ".....rds.amazonaws.com"
rds_database_name = "c360db"
rds_endpoint = "....rds.amazonaws.com:5432"
rds_port = 5432
secrets_manager_secret_arn = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:....."
vpc_cidr_block = "10......"
vpc_id = "vpc-...."

Once the database is up and running, the backend creates the tables, the c360_cdc_publication, and seeds the committed CSV dataset on startup — there is no separate schema/seed script. Build DATABASE_URL from the RDS secret and run the backend bootstrap (or just start the API):

# Pull the RDS credentials emitted into Secrets Manager by Terraform
export RDSHOST="c360-....rds.amazonaws.com"
export DB_PASSWORD=$(aws secretsmanager get-secret-value \
  --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:...:secret:c360-... \
  --query SecretString --output text | jq -r .password)

cd apps/backend
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://dbadmin:${DB_PASSWORD}@${RDSHOST}:5432/c360db?sslmode=require" \
uv run python bootstrap.py

The bootstrap is idempotent, so it is safe to re-run. The CDC publication now covers all three tables (customers, accounts, transactions).

docs.title: Some info
docs.text:
• AWS RDS requires a DB Subnet Group. RDS manages its own Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). An RDS instance requires a DB Subnet Group defining a pool of subnets across at least two different Availability Zones (AZs) in that VPC (even for Single-AZ instances, so AWS can perform maintenance, failover, or migrations).
  • The aws_db_instance resource only accepts db_subnet_group_name, not individual subnet IDs

To retrieve password from secret, knowing the secret arn do: 

aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-west-2:.....:secret:c360-j9r-rds-credentials-9x --query SecretString --output text |jq -r .password
